clue.text: But these students aren't always on the same social plane

definitions.text: But these students aren't always on the same social plane

parts.words: But these students aren't always on the same social plane
parts.note: pupils taught together in one form share a school grade, yet in society they may come from quite different classes

explanation.surface: A remark on how fellow pupils can come from very different backgrounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The pun is on 'class': a school class shares a year, a social class shares a rank, and those taught together need not share the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils who share a school form are, by that fact alone, fellows of the same class.

clue.text: Sea-food caught in error

explanation.surface: A seafood dish was ordered by mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: In rowing, to 'catch a crab' is a mistimed stroke in which the oar jams in the water, so this creature is what an oarsman catches in error.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea-food: a shellfish eaten at table; caught in error: the rowing blunder of jamming the oar is called catching one.

clue.text: Financial help for a go ahead concern?

definitions.text: Financial help for a go ahead concern?

parts.words: Financial help for a go ahead concern?
parts.note: money paid up front as a loan, and the very word for going ahead, so it suits an enterprising firm twice over

explanation.surface: Asking what sort of funding a thriving, enterprising company should get.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go-ahead' looks like a description of a dynamic firm; it also names the answer's verb sense, to move forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A loan paid before it is earned is called this, and the word also means to move forward, as an enterprising business does.

clue.text: A woman of parts

parts.note: 'of parts' usually means talented, but here it means one who played many stage roles

explanation.surface: Praise for an accomplished, many-talented lady.
explanation.walkthrough: SARAH SIDDONS (1755-1831) was the most celebrated English tragic actress of her day; 'parts' are her theatrical roles.
explanation.definitionFit: She was a famous Georgian stage actress, a performer of many dramatic roles such as Lady Macbeth.

clue.text: Tamed in a lively way

indicators.note: as in 'in a bad way', the letters are put into a different state, signalling that they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something wild has been domesticated, yet stays spirited.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of TAMED IN A are rearranged; 'lively' is the definition, and 'way' tells the solver the fodder is put into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of life and spirit, a direct synonym.

clue.text: One thing one is not liable to be

definitions.text: One thing one is not liable to be

parts.words: One thing one is not liable to be
parts.note: being not liable, for tax or duty, is exactly the state described, so the clue defines itself

explanation.surface: A wry remark about something a person is unlikely ever to become.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not liable to be' reads as 'unlikely to be', but taken literally it means 'free from liability', which is the answer's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone free from an obligation such as tax or military service is not liable for it.

clue.text: A blunder, either way

indicators.note: the word for the mistake reads the same whichever direction it is spelt

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A mistake whichever way you look at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either way' tells you the answer is a palindrome, the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British word for a silly mistake.

clue.text: Antony didn't claim to be one of these

definitions.text: Antony didn't claim to be one of these

parts.words: Antony didn't claim to be one of these
parts.note: Mark Antony in Julius Caesar says 'I am no orator, as Brutus is' before his great funeral speech

explanation.surface: A modest disclaimer by a man called Antony.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference is Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, where Mark Antony falsely protests that he is no public speaker before swaying the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Public speakers, which Antony modestly denied being in his funeral speech for Caesar.

clue.text: Acrimony has a certain attraction for some drinkers

definitions.text: a certain attraction for some drinkers

explanation.surface: Resentment has its appeal to a certain kind of drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British draught beer, so its quality draws those who drink it; the same word means resentful hostility.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimony: rancour and resentment; the attraction: the sharp, hoppy taste that bitter-beer drinkers enjoy.

clue.text: He may have his own ideas on hoarding

definitions.text: He may have his own ideas on hoarding

parts.words: He may have his own ideas on hoarding
parts.note: a hoarding is a British billboard, so a firm putting its promotions on one has its ideas displayed there

explanation.surface: Someone with personal opinions about stockpiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarding' looks like stockpiling, but in British English it is a large outdoor billboard.
explanation.definitionFit: One who promotes goods, often with posters on billboards.

clue.text: Ain't she sweet-if no better than she should be ?

definitions.text: Ain't she sweet-if no better than she should be

parts.words: Ain't she sweet-if no better than she should be
parts.note: a pastry dessert is a sweet, and the same word is slang for a woman of loose morals

explanation.surface: A line from the song Ain't She Sweet, with a sly doubt about the lady's virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'a sweet' is a dessert; the answer is a pastry one, and also old slang for a promiscuous woman, 'no better than she should be'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit pastry served as dessert, and also derogatory slang for a woman thought promiscuous.

clue.text: Where does Nanny's Pa live, confound it ?

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the preceding words are jumbled

parts.note: the possessive S counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: An exasperated question about where a nanny's father lives.
explanation.walkthrough: NANNYS PA LIVE, twelve letters, are rearranged; 'confound it' reads as an oath but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A place, the US state, answering the question 'where'.

clue.text: One of four in hand

parts.note: a hand, used to measure horses, is four units of length, so each is one of the four

explanation.surface: One of four cards held in a player's hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' is not the one at the end of your arm or at cards but the horse-height measure of four inches.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of length, a twelfth of a foot; a horse-measuring hand contains four.

clue.text: Fruit centre

parts.note: the middle of a pippin or russet, left uneaten

explanation.surface: A place where fruit is sold or stored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit centre' suggests a market or depot, but it is simply the middle of the fruit that is thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: The tough inner part of a pippin, holding its seeds, left after eating.

clue.text: No shipping company would care to deposit its assets here

definitions.text: No shipping company would care to deposit its assets here

parts.words: No shipping company would care to deposit its assets here
parts.note: a bank is where assets are deposited, but this is a sandbank in the North Sea where ships run aground

explanation.surface: A remark on where a shipping firm would never choose to keep its money.
explanation.walkthrough: DOGGER BANK is a large shallow sandbank in the North Sea, named in the British shipping forecast; vessels landing there would lose their cargo.
explanation.definitionFit: A North Sea sandbank, dangerous to vessels, and a 'bank' only in the geographical sense.

clue.text: Partial, like a government without an opposition

definitions.text: like a government without an opposition

explanation.surface: Describing a biased regime that permits no rival party.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from 'side': biased towards one side, and having only one side in a parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Partial: biased, favouring one view; a government without opposition has only a single party in the chamber.

clue.text: The noun is, in this form, concord

indicators.note: the letters are taken and given another shape, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on agreement between a noun and its verb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concord' is a grammar term for agreement, fitting the noun-and-verb surface; here it means harmony. NOUN IS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreement or harmony, as when all sing or act together.

clue.text: Theatre advertisement-setting out production cost? .

explanation.surface: A theatre poster that details how much the show cost to stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A bill is an invoice, so the bill for a play would state what the production cost; the answer is also a theatre poster.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre advertisement: a poster announcing a show; the second reading is an invoice for a stage production.

clue.text: Such a person doesn't easily get fed-up

definitions.text: Such a person doesn't easily get fed-up

parts.words: Such a person doesn't easily get fed-up
parts.note: 'fed-up' read literally means having had enough to eat, which a glutton never does

explanation.surface: Praise for someone patient who rarely becomes bored or annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed-up' looks like 'annoyed', but taken literally it means sated with food.
explanation.definitionFit: A glutton or avaricious person always wants more and is never sated.

clue.text: She 'might sell tea for a change

indicators.note: the letters are altered in order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman might take up selling tea as a change of job.
explanation.walkthrough: ESTELLA is the heroine of Dickens's Great Expectations. SELL TEA is rearranged; 'She' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name, borne by the cold heroine of Great Expectations.

clue.text: Those cast in juvenile roles ?

parts.note: boys who act in a play, and also pleasure-seeking men who behave like youths

explanation.surface: Actors chosen to play young characters.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer split in two is boys in a play; whole, it means idle rich men who act immaturely.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy pleasure-seekers, who play the part of irresponsible youths.

clue.text: Where is the team that has already batted ?

definitions.text: Where is the team that has already batted

parts.words: Where is the team that has already batted
parts.note: in cricket the batting side is 'in', so the side that has finished batting is 'out'

explanation.surface: A cricket question about where the side that has batted is now.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is a British summer game: the batting team is 'in', and the side whose innings is done is the out side, in the field.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the team not batting is called the out side; the word also means beyond the walls.

clue.text: Chirpy little creature about to embrace one, the rotter

indicators.note: the abbreviation for about holds the other pieces inside it as in a hug

parts.note: CA is short for circa, about
I is the Roman numeral for one
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rotter

explanation.surface: A small cheerful animal is about to hug someone who behaves badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to embrace' reads as 'on the point of hugging', but 'about' gives CA, and 'to embrace' puts I and CAD inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud-chirping insect, small and noisy in summer heat.

clue.text: Characteristic of a great all-rounder ?

parts.note: an all-rounder is a cricketer good at batting and bowling, but here it is someone round all over, that is fat

explanation.surface: The quality that marks out a great cricketer who bats and bowls.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an all-rounder excels at both batting and bowling; the clue reads it literally, as someone very round.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumpness or roundness of figure, the quality of being round all over.

clue.text: A word of no significance :

parts.note: not a meaningless word but one that signifies 'no', a refusal or ban

explanation.surface: A remark about a trivial, meaningless word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of no significance' looks like 'unimportant'; read as 'signifying no', it is the Latin for 'I forbid'.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal refusal or ban, from the Latin 'I forbid', signifying no.

clue.text: Just the fellow to be keen on a pun

definitions.text: Just the fellow to be keen on a pun

parts.words: Just the fellow to be keen on a pun
parts.note: this man placed after the word 'pun' makes a word meaning sharp or keen, as of a strong smell

explanation.surface: A man who seems the type to enjoy wordplay.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'on a pun' as 'added to the word PUN': this man written after it gives PUNGENT, which means keen.
explanation.definitionFit: A short informal word for a gentleman, that is a fellow.

clue.text: Entirely happy ending, with him in one's league

parts.note: all means wholly, entirely

indicators.note: the word's ending is its final letter

explanation.surface: A thoroughly happy conclusion, with a man joining your team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'happy ending' looks like a story's conclusion, but it means the last letter of 'happy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A partner or confederate is someone in league with you.

clue.text: Extent of TV broadcast, after the news

definitions.text: Extent of TV broadcast, after the news

parts.words: Extent of TV broadcast, after the news
parts.note: a programme reaching the whole country, and the name of a BBC magazine show screened after the early evening news

explanation.surface: How far a television transmission reaches once the bulletin is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Nationwide was a BBC current-affairs programme broadcast after the evening news in the 1970s; the word also means across the whole country.
explanation.definitionFit: Covering the whole country, as a broadcast across all regions does.

clue.text: A bit of a back-hander for the governor

indicators.note: only a part of the following word is taken, so the letters are found inside it

explanation.surface: A small bribe paid to an official.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'back-hander' is a British word for a bribe, apt for a governor; the answer is inside 'bacK-HANder'.
explanation.definitionFit: A title for a ruler or chief in Central Asia and India.

clue.text: Strangely menial part of government

indicators.note: the words are arranged in an odd way, so their letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A humble role within the state's administration.
explanation.walkthrough: MENIAL PART is rearranged; the held text repeated 'government' by an OCR slip, and the page prints 'part of government'.
explanation.definitionFit: The legislative assembly, the body that makes law and governs.
